searches.note: Twenty four searches of a share of twenty eight, four left unspent, none of them the author's. Seven were restricted to a house's own domain or a reference body (tyrrells.com.au once, mountpleasantwines.com.au once, brokenwood.com.au once, lakesfolly.wine twice, one of them with two merchants, thomaswines.com.au twice) and adb.anu.edu.au once; the rest kept the house's domain out where the author had leant on it, so that each second source would be independent. One search on Lake's Folly's making returned nothing of the house and is counted all the same. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

History went first to the Australian Dictionary of Biography, the Newcastle Herald, the Guardian's obituary and the trade with the house's domain kept out; the making, the sites and the release went to the house's own pages and to merchants' sheets.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check, or in one only that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less, and the house's own claims are told as its record.

The dead are named with their dates where two sources agree (Dan Tyrrell, 1871 to 1959, by the ADB and the Newcastle Herald; Murray Tyrrell, 1921 to 2000; Maurice O'Shea, 1897 to 1956, by the ADB, Wikipedia and the National Portrait Gallery; Max Lake, 1924 to 2009, by Wikipedia and the Guardian's notice of his death on 14 April 2009, aged 84). Edward Tyrrell, the founder, had only a death year in one source and is now described.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Chris Shanahan, Campbell Mattinson, Wine with Seth, Jancis Robinson's) are cited neither in the fragment nor as a second source here. The serving temperatures agree with the service reference: light whites 7 to 10 for the two Semillons, medium reds 15 to 17 for the two Shiraz and the Cabernets.

tested: Dan Tyrrell, 1871 to 1959, first wine in 1885 at fourteen, last in 1959, ran the winery after his father died in 1909: the ADB. Confirmed. The count of vintages is 74 in the ADB, 75 in the Newcastle Herald and 69 in two others, and 1885 to 1959 counts seventy five. Cut.

The founder: came out in 1850 (the ADB, with the Newcastle Herald, which has him come with two brothers), took up land at Pokolbin in 1858 and built a slab hut (the ADB, the house, the Newcastle Herald), first vintage 1864 (the ADB, the Herald, the house). Confirmed. His birth was found nowhere and his death year in the ADB alone; the planting of 1861 in no source of this check. Described, and 1861 cut.
Murray Tyrrell took over in 1959 and kept the chosen wines for the family's label, where almost all had been sold to other wineries: the Newcastle Herald and a trade wiki. Confirmed.

Chardonnay planted in 1968 from cuttings taken in 1967, a trial in 1970, the first Vat 47 in 1971, named for the number of its cask: the Newcastle Herald and the trade; Lake's Folly's own account dates its Chardonnay of 1969 a year after Murray Tyrrell's. Confirmed; the first commercial varietal Chardonnay is Tyrrell's claim and contested, so it is told as the house's count.

Short Flat, first planted in 1923 on its own roots, with vines of 1923 and 1927 the backbone of Vat 1: the house's 2019 note, The Wine Independent and Decanter. Confirmed; always is softened to at its heart.

The making (hand picked, lightly pressed, free run juice fermented cool in stainless steel, about six weeks on fine lees, bottled in June): the house's 2026 notes. Confirmed as primary; dry grown and own rooted vines by its 2021 page.

The first vintage of Vat 1: 1962 by one review, 1963 under the name Hunter River Riesling by Langton's, 1989 by a merchant who confuses it with a later generation. Unsettled; the story's 1960s stands.

The questions: the Vat 47 question had the founder as a distractor, impossible on its face since he died in 1909; it is now Max Lake, who planted Chardonnay a year later. The rules: no living name (the founder's great grandson stays undescribed in the record), no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: Edward Tyrrell, an English emigrant who died in 1909, took up land at Pokolbin in 1858, lived at first in a slab hut and planted vines in 1861; the house dates its first vintage to 1864. His son Dan Tyrrell (1871 to 1959) made his first wine in 1885, at fourteen, and his last in 1959, seventy four vintages in a row, running the winery after his father's death while a brother cared for the vines. Until then most of the wine was sold to other wineries. Murray Tyrrell (1921 to 2000), a grandson of the founder, took over in 1959 and began to keep the chosen wines for the family's own label. In the 1960s he set them apart as the Winemaker's Selection, each named for the vat that held it, and Vat 1 was the Semillon. He planted Chardonnay in 1968, and its first wine, Vat 47 of 1971, is credited as the first commercial varietal Chardonnay of Australia. Vat 1 kept to the old Hunter way: picked early, fermented in steel and never touched by oak, so that its toast and lanolin come from the bottle alone. For a sommelier it is the standing proof that a hot, humid valley can make a light, long lived dry white.
changed.now: The founder, an English emigrant who had come out in 1850, took up land at Pokolbin in 1858 and built a slab hut there; the house and the Australian Dictionary of Biography both date his first vintage to 1864. His son Dan Tyrrell (1871 to 1959) made his first wine in 1885, at fourteen, and his last in 1959, running the winery after his father's death in 1909 while a brother helped with the vines. Until then most of the wine was sold to other wineries. Murray Tyrrell (1921 to 2000), a grandson of the founder, took over in 1959 and began to keep the chosen wines for the family's own label. In the 1960s he set them apart as the Winemaker's Selection, each named for the vat or cask that held it, and Vat 1 was the Semillon. He planted Chardonnay in 1968, and its first wine, Vat 47 of 1971, is counted by the house as the first commercial varietal Chardonnay of Australia, a claim others have contested. Vat 1 kept to the old Hunter way: picked early, fermented in steel and never touched by oak, so that its toast and lanolin come from the bottle alone. For a sommelier it is the standing proof that a hot, humid valley can make a light, long lived dry white.
changed.why: The founder's dates were not found in two sources (birth nowhere, death in the ADB alone), so he is described; the 1861 planting rested on no source of this check; seventy four vintages conflicts with its own years and with other accounts; Vat 47's first is the house's claim and is contested.

tested: Maurice O'Shea, 1897 to 1956: the ADB, Wikipedia (13 June 1897 to 5 May 1956) and the National Portrait Gallery. Confirmed; one listing gives 5 March.
Studied at Montpellier and in Paris, home in 1920 at his mother's request, the name Mount Pleasant given in 1925: the ADB, with the National Portrait Gallery on the naming. Confirmed; Paris added.
A half share to McWilliam's in 1932, the rest in 1941, still manager and winemaker: the ADB and the trade. Confirmed.

Born in North Sydney, the son of an Irish wine merchant and a French mother, president of the Newcastle branch of the Wine and Food Society, died of cancer at his flat in Newcastle: the ADB alone. The founding of the society in 1939 is not in the ADB's own summary. All cut.

Old Hill planted in 1880 beneath the Brokenback Range; Old Paddock in 1921 from its cuttings on deep red volcanic loam; Rosehill in 1946; eighteen months in large French oak barrels; first made in 1987 and released in 1990: the house's history and vineyard pages. Confirmed as primary; Rosehill is 1945 in Langton's.

Made only in exceptional vintages, a selection of barrels from Old Hill, Old Paddock and Rosehill, Old Hill on heavy volcanic soil: Langton's, Prince Wine Store and two other merchants, one of which adds the 1965 vines. Confirmed; the three vineyards become above all.
Five hundred metres apart: in no source of this check. Cut.
The rules: the present winemaker and the critics the house quotes stay unnamed; the house's own pages quote a living critic's rating, which the record does not carry. Sound.

changed.was: Shiraz has grown on the hill at Pokolbin since 1880, when an earlier settler planted the Old Hill vineyard on volcanic soil beneath the Brokenback Range. Maurice O'Shea (1897 to 1956), born in North Sydney, studied wine in France at Montpellier and came home in 1920 at his mother's request. By the house's account the family bought the property in 1921, and he planted Old Paddock that year from cuttings of Old Hill; the Australian Dictionary of Biography dates the name Mount Pleasant to 1925. In the Depression, in 1932, he sold a half share to McWilliam's and stayed on as manager and winemaker, and in 1941 he sold the rest and went on making the wine. He helped found the Wine and Food Society of New South Wales in 1939, planted Rosehill in 1946 and died in Newcastle in 1956. In 1987 the estate made the first Maurice O'Shea Shiraz, a selection from Old Hill, Old Paddock and Rosehill, bottled only in strong years. For a sommelier it ties O'Shea's name to the medium bodied, long lived Shiraz the Hunter is known for, from vines he planted or tended himself.
changed.now: Shiraz has grown on the hill at Pokolbin since 1880, when an earlier settler planted the Old Hill vineyard on volcanic soil beneath the Brokenback Range. Maurice O'Shea (1897 to 1956) studied wine in France, at Montpellier and in Paris, and came home in 1920 at his mother's request. By the house's account the family bought the property in 1921, and he planted Old Paddock that year from cuttings of Old Hill; the Australian Dictionary of Biography dates the name Mount Pleasant to 1925. In the Depression, in 1932, he sold a half share to McWilliam's and stayed on as manager and winemaker, and in 1941 he sold the rest and went on making the wine. He planted Rosehill in 1946 and remained the estate's winemaker until his death in 1956. In 1987 the estate made the first Maurice O'Shea Shiraz, a selection drawn above all from Old Hill, Old Paddock and Rosehill, released in 1990 and bottled only in strong years. For a sommelier it ties O'Shea's name to the medium bodied, long lived Shiraz the Hunter is known for, from vines he planted or tended himself.
changed.why: Three details rested on the ADB alone, and the founding of the society is not in its summary; Paris is in the ADB with Montpellier; the flagship draws on more than the three vineyards in one merchant's account; the release year is the house's.

tested: Founded in 1970 by three Sydney solicitors on a block once destined for a cricket ground; first vintage 1973; six new partners in 1978 and the Graveyard bought, planted in 1968; earmarked as a cemetery for the parish and never used; first single vineyard Shiraz in 1983 by the winemaker who joined in 1982: Decanter, the trade and a regional magazine with the house's domain kept out. Confirmed.
Six of thirty five vintages declassified, among them the 2016: the house's post of 2018. Confirmed as the house's count, now said so.
Heavy clay: the house's Verona page compares Verona's heavy clay with the Graveyard's. Confirmed; one page of the house says red volcanic, left open.

The making: open fermenters of two or three tonnes by the house's older and later notes; 2001 in new oak, seventy per cent French and thirty American; 2017 for eighteen months in mostly large seasoned French puncheons and a cask of three thousand litres; up to fourteen months by Langton's, twelve to fourteen by a sommelier reference; 2022 with no new oak. Corrected to twelve to eighteen months; the warm fermentation, the cold soak and the 2018 in seasoned oak alone were in no source of this check and are cut.

ILR Reserve Semillon: unoaked, released at six years, under screwcap, by a merchant quoting the winemaker and the house's flagship page. Confirmed; little or no skin contact was in no source and is cut. HBA Shiraz: the house's flagship trio and a merchant. Confirmed.

The rules: the founders, one of them a living critic, and the winemakers stay unnamed; the ILR and HBA names stand as the wines' names; a critic's score and a Winery of the Year award met among the results are not carried. Sound.

changed.was: Fermented warm in small open fermenters, often after a short cold soak, the wine is matured for well over a year in French oak, from barriques to larger puncheons. The shares of new and of American oak have fallen over the years, and some vintages, 2018 and 2022 among them, used seasoned French oak alone. In weak years the wine is declassified and not released as Graveyard.
changed.now: Fermented in small open fermenters, the wine is matured for twelve to eighteen months, by vintage, in French oak. New French and American barriques once had a large share; the house has moved towards seasoned French puncheons and larger casks, with no new oak at all in 2022. In weak years the wine is declassified and not released as Graveyard.
changed.why: Well over a year overstated the shortest regimes; the warm fermentation, the cold soak and the 2018 claim had no source; the oak's shift is told by the sheets of 2001, 2017 and 2022.

changed.was: In 1970 three Sydney lawyers, who claimed little knowledge of viticulture, bought a small block at Pokolbin that had once been meant for a cricket ground. They planted Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon in 1971 and picked their first vintage in 1973. In 1978 six new partners joined the venture, which made it possible to buy the neighbouring vineyard, planted to Shiraz in 1968. It was called the Graveyard because the Pokolbin parish map marked it as the Cemetery Block, though it was never used as one. Its heavy clay was hard to work, but its fruit stood apart, and in 1983, the first vintage of a new winemaker, the house began to bottle its single vineyard wines, the Graveyard Shiraz among them. The partnership grew, yet the Graveyard stayed a wine of one site, and the house declassifies it in weak years: six of its first thirty five vintages were not sold under the name. For a sommelier it is Pokolbin Shiraz of one vineyard, fragrant and medium bodied, from a house that began as three lawyers' venture and became one of the names a guest knows in the Hunter.

changed.was: Max Lake (1924 to 2009) was a Sydney surgeon, the first in Australia to specialise in surgery of the hand. In 1963 his family and friends planted Cabernet Sauvignon on a block at Pokolbin, in a valley known for Semillon and Shiraz, and the vines of that first planting, Block 1, stand in front of the cellar door. By the house's account the first vintage came in 1966, made largely by hand, and Chardonnay followed in 1969. A small estate making wine from its own vines alone, Lake's Folly is often called the first boutique winery of modern Australia. The founder's son became its winemaker in 1973, and Max Lake left surgery in 1979 to give himself to wine and food. In early 2000 the family sold the estate to a Perth businessman, and the Cabernets comes from the same single vineyard. Its blend moves with the year, led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Shiraz, Merlot and Petit Verdot beside it, and a guest remembers it for perfume and fine tannin rather than weight. For a sommelier it answers the guess that the Hunter grows only Semillon and Shiraz: Cabernet of restraint, from a surgeon's folly that lasted.

changed.was: The Braemore vineyard was planted to Semillon in 1969 beside Hermitage Road at Pokolbin, on a narrow band of sandy alluvial soil laid down by an ancient watercourse. The house's founder grew up in McLaren Vale, the son of a winemaker there, and came to the Hunter in 1987 to join Tyrrell's, where over some thirteen years he rose to red winemaker. In 1997 he released the first wine under his own name, choosing to make only the Hunter's two signature grapes, Semillon and Shiraz, and two years later he left Tyrrell's to set up on his own at Pokolbin. For the 2000 vintage the young house first bought a small parcel of Braemore fruit, and the single vineyard Semillon it made became its flagship white. It went on buying the fruit for nearly two decades, and in December 2017, when the vineyard's owners decided to sell, Thomas Wines bought Braemore outright. The wine keeps to the Hunter's old way, early picking, steel and no oak, and the house releases a Cellar Reserve of it with years in bottle. For a sommelier it is the modern face of Hunter Semillon: a single vineyard long in a grower's hands, made by a winemaker trained at Tyrrell's, and proof that the style carries on in new hands.
